Comprehensive experimental ablations validating design choices: two-phase generation analysis (Section 4.2), guided vs. unguided comparison (Section 4.3), and systematic hyperparameter studies (Appendix C)
Demonstrates practical improvements across multiple domains: text generation (OpenWebText), code generation (Conala), and instruction-tuned LLMs (Dream-Instruct 7B)
Parameter-efficient design: lightweight error predictor (single head training) adds negligible overhead while achieving significant gains in medium-step regimes

Fundamental limitation of star-shaped approach: pure star-shaped sampling fails, requiring hybrid MDLM+Star design for only final 20-40% of generation, suggesting core method has significant limitations
Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing empirical comparisons with GIDD, informed correctors, and other recent discrete diffusion guidance methods despite citing them

Insufficient error predictor analysis: no metrics on detection accuracy, false positive rates, or sensitivity to model changes; single Figure 7 example for qualitative validation

Missing computational cost analysis: no inference time comparison, refinement loops add steps but overhead not quantified; no analysis of computational fairness vs. ReMDM

Limited experimental scope: modest model scale (Dream-Instruct 7B), no human evaluation, no failure case analysis, max sequence length only 1280 tokens, no comparison with continuous latent diffusion approaches
Hyperparameter sensitivity remains: despite ReMDM improvements, τ_remask still requires tuning (Figure 6 shows optimal range T≈4-32); 10% loop size is heuristic-based

strengths: Sound mathematical framework with rigorous proof (Claim 1) that star-shaped VLB simplifies to weighted cross-entropy compatible with pretrained models
Comprehensive experimental design with extensive ablations on activation time, guided vs. unguided sampling, loop schedules, and error predictor capacity
Honest discussion of limitations (inability to handle insertion/deletion, separate error predictor training required)
Clear presentation of algorithms and thorough reproducibility information with promised source code and public datasets
Well-structured analysis of generative phases, demonstrating that pure star-shaped sampling fails early but succeeds late (Section 4.2)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Star-shaped formulation is mathematically equivalent to ReMDM (acknowledged), with the only contribution being replacement of random remasking with a learned error predictor—a straightforward supervised learning task without methodological innovation

Improvements are conditional and marginal: Most pronounced gains occur only in very constrained 32-128 step regimes; at 512 steps, G-Star-loop's MAUVE score (58.6) actually decreases compared to 256 steps (60.9) due to quality-diversity tradeoff, severely limiting practical applicability

Downstream benchmark improvements are modest (1-3 points on Dream-Instruct tasks, Table 3) without statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or discussion of whether gains are within noise margins

Incomplete analysis of error prediction: Missing investigation of how error predictor trained at random noise levels transfers to structured inference sequences, no ablation on error label quality, and no visualization of learned error patterns

Unfair experimental comparison: ReMDM's high hyperparameter sensitivity to η (Figure 4) suggests optimal-tuned ReMDM may not have received equal optimization effort; missing comparisons with other recent refinement methods (GIDD, informed correctors, Schiff et al. 2024 guidance mechanisms)

Method adds significant complexity: Requires separate training stage for each task/domain (demonstrated across OWT, Conala, Tulu 3), introduces new hyperparameter τ_remask with non-monotonic effects, and inference computational overhead is not discussed
Weak baseline MDLM performance in Table 1 (5.4 MAUVE at 128 steps) raises questions about setup validity; unclear whether improvements stem from the method or experimental confounds

Disconnect between identified problem and proposed solution: Section 4.2 diagnoses early-stage 'generative incoherence' from generating mutually incoherent tokens, but targeted error remasking addresses token-level correctness rather than coherence—the mechanism's relevance to the diagnosed problem is unclear

strengths: Clear problem formulation: The paper effectively articulates the fundamental limitation of masked diffusion—irreversible token commitment preventing error correction—and provides compelling motivation.

Solid theoretical foundation: The star-shaped reformulation (Eq. 4) is mathematically clean; Claim 1's proof correctly shows compatibility with pre-trained models via weighted cross-entropy objective; mathematical connection to ReMDM is well-established.

Insightful two-phase decomposition: Discovery that pure star-shaped sampling fails early due to coherence degradation is valuable; hybrid MDLM→Star strategy is well-motivated and empirically validated (Figures 1-2, ton≈0.3 optimal).
Parameter-efficient error predictor: Lightweight head-only fine-tuning on frozen representations achieves competitive performance; ablation study (Table 1) demonstrates 12B,H nearly matches 12B,F.

Comprehensive experimental analysis: Systematic ablations on activation time, loop size, predictor temperature; detailed analysis of ReMDM hyperparameter brittleness (Figure 4); multi-domain evaluation across text, code, and instruction-tuned models with multiple metrics.

Practical advantages: Works with pre-trained MDLMs without fine-tuning; simple 10% refinement heuristic generalizes across tasks; outperforms ReMDM without extensive per-schedule tuning (Appendix C.1 quantifies ReMDM brittleness).

Excellent presentation: Clear writing, logical flow, insightful visualizations (especially Figures 8-9 showing structured vs. random remasking patterns); detailed appendix with implementation details and code availability.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: The star-shaped formulation is from Okhotin et al. (2023); the error predictor is a straightforward binary classification model trained on oracle labels. Main contribution combines existing ideas rather than fundamental innovation.

Missing error predictor analysis: No quantitative evaluation of error predictor performance (precision, recall, calibration, confusion matrix); qualitative evidence only (Appendix E); no analysis of out-of-distribution errors or domain shift (Dream-Instruct error predictor trained on Tulu 3, not target domain).

Modest improvements on larger models: Dream-Instruct gains are only 1-2 points on most benchmarks (Table 3); no statistical significance testing or error bars; marginal improvements on complex reasoning tasks (GPQA, HumanEval), raising scalability concerns.

Quality-diversity trade-off unresolved: Consistent diversity reduction across experiments; MAUVE scores decrease at 512 steps vs. 256 steps (57.3→56.3); explanation in Appendix C.2 is post-hoc rather than predictive; no clear guidance on quality vs. diversity trade-offs.
Computational cost under-specified: No wall-clock time comparisons provided; 10% refinement overhead not quantified; latency implications for deployed systems unclear.
In-place substitution limitation: Cannot fix insertion/deletion errors (acknowledged in Appendix G), limiting real-world error correction capability.
Incomplete baseline comparisons: No comparison to GIDD (von Rutte et al., 2025) despite mentioning it as an alternative; missing comparisons to recent flow-matching or other discrete methods.

Analysis of star-shaped failure incomplete: Explanation for why pure star-shaped fails relies on step-to-step similarity as proxy metric; no rigorous testing of 'generative incoherence' hypothesis; mechanistic understanding lacking.

Implementation details gaps: Nucleus probability (pnucleus, Algorithm 2) used but unexplained; hyperparameter choices (e.g., 15 tokens for Dream-Instruct) lack justification; some parameters in code but not in text.
Reproducibility limitations: Results appear to be single runs with no error bars or confidence intervals; no ablation on sensitivity to hyperparameter choices like nucleus filter threshold.

strengths: Sound theoretical framework with formal proof of VLB simplification (Claim 1) and elegant connection to ReMDM (Proposition 1), enabling reuse of pre-trained weights without fine-tuning

Compelling two-phase generation insight (Section 4.2): systematic analysis identifying that star-shaped sampling should only apply in late stages (~30% of steps) while preserving stability of early context-building phase
Principled error predictor design trained on actual diffusion errors rather than synthetic noise, addressing key limitation of confidence-based methods relying on miscalibrated confidence scores

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple domains (OWT, Conala, instruction-tuned 7B) with principled Pareto frontier analysis, extensive ablations on loop size/temperature/capacity, and strong out-of-domain robustness (AUC-ROC ≥0.84)

Consistent improvements across 7 diverse benchmarks (Table 1: +1.3 to +2.9 points) and superior performance in medium-step regimes (64-256 steps), with clear advantages at 128 steps over full-budget baselines
Excellent presentation with clear algorithms, comprehensive appendices, practical guidance for hyperparameter tuning, and informative visualizations (especially Appendix F remasking pattern analysis)
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to ReMDM: method is mathematically equivalent to ReMDM with σ_t = 1 - α_{t-1}, with core novelty being learned guidance instead of heuristic scheduling; concurrent work (Kim et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025) explores similar directions but receives limited discussion

Modest improvements in high-step regimes: at 512 steps, improvements narrow significantly; on Conala code generation (Table 2), gains over ReMDM are incremental; gains of ~1-3 MMLU points are useful but not dramatic

Significant practical overhead: 50% latency increase for 12B,H variant (3.43s vs 2.26s); 192 vs 128 NFEs for better-quality models; requires task-specific error predictor training (different datasets for different models), limiting claimed 'universality'

Theoretical gaps in early-stage coherence loss: Section 4.2 provides intuition but lacks formal analysis of why x_t independence causes degradation; distributional alignment between training (ground truth x₀ available) and inference (errors unknown) not rigorously justified

Acknowledged limitations reduce applicability: cannot perform insertion/deletion (only in-place substitution); requires separate sequential error predictor training; no aggressive throughput optimization; these meaningfully constrain real-world deployment

Experimental and methodological concerns: out-of-domain evaluation uses only text domains (no code→math or more distant shifts); hyperparameter sensitivity acknowledged but remains high (multiple temperatures and scheduling parameters); Pareto frontier in Figure 4 is busy and difficult to parse

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation with thorough ablations across multiple datasets and metrics (OWT, Conala, Dream-Instruct)
Practical error predictor design with parameter-efficient head-only training and detailed computational cost analysis
Clear presentation with effective visualizations of refinement dynamics (Figures 1-2, 9-10) providing good intuition
Mathematically sound formulation with correct proofs of claims and connection to ReMDM
Cross-domain generalization study (Table 3) showing AUC-ROC ≥0.90 despite training on single dataset
Pareto frontier analysis enables more informative method comparison than single-point evaluations
weaknesses: Fundamental issue with core approach: pure star-shaped sampling produces degenerate text (near-zero MAUVE), addressed via hybrid switching rather than principled solution—theoretical explanation for why conditional independence causes degradation is missing
Limited novelty: primarily combines existing ideas (Okhotin et al.'s star-shaped paradigm, remasking, binary error classification) without significant new conceptual insights
Modest empirical improvements relative to overhead: +1-3 points on most benchmarks, improvements narrow at higher step counts, no statistical significance testing despite stochastic sampling

Incomplete baseline comparisons: ReMDM shown to be sensitive to tuning (Appendix C.1), but unclear if G-Star has also been optimized fairly; no comparison to concurrent work (Kim et al., Huang et al. 2025); no end-to-end out-of-domain evaluation despite cross-domain AUC-ROC analysis
Method adds non-trivial complexity and overhead: requires separate training of error predictor, ~50% latency increase (Table 4), limited to in-place substitutions only

Missing critical analysis: no human evaluation despite modest automatic metric improvements, no failure mode analysis, 'step-to-step similarity' metric is proxy-based, no ablation on key choices (nucleus filtering, temperature schedules, 10% refinement budget in Dream experiments)

Training-inference mismatch justification (Section 3.2) is reasonable but deserves deeper analysis beyond intuitive explanation; claim about synthetic noise limitations needs stronger empirical support

strengths: Well-motivated problem with a clear solution: Addresses the irreversibility limitation of masked diffusion through a theoretically grounded star-shaped paradigm

Strong experimental validation across multiple domains: Convincing improvements on few-step generation (4× step reduction while beating full-budget baselines), comprehensive benchmarks, Pareto frontier analysis, and robustness studies

Key practical insight about two-phase generation: The empirical demonstration that early stages require stable context-building while late stages benefit from refinement is conceptually valuable and well-validated

Superior error correction approach: Training the error predictor on actual diffusion errors rather than synthetic noise is more principled and demonstrates clear advantages over confidence-based and uniform-noise baselines
Excellent presentation and reproducibility: Clear writing, well-organized structure, extensive appendices with implementation details, public code, and honest limitations discussion
Parameter-efficient design: Head-only variant achieves near-optimal performance with negligible parameter overhead, enabling practical deployment
Theoretical soundness: Claim 1 and Proposition 1 correctly establish compatibility with pre-trained models and connection to ReMDM
weaknesses: Moderate novelty: Combines existing ideas (star-shaped diffusion from Okhotin et al., standard error detection, two-phase scheduling) rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts

Inconsistent framing of practical requirements: Claims 'plug-and-play' operation with pre-trained models but requires ~48 hours of separate error predictor training on H200, not truly parameter-free adaptation

Modest downstream benchmark improvements: Table 1 shows consistent but small gains (+1.3 to +2.9 points), limiting practical significance for real-world applications despite strong perplexity improvements
Limited concurrent work comparison: Kim et al. (2025) and Huang et al. (2025) are acknowledged but not experimentally compared despite addressing the same problem
Missing human evaluation: All evaluation is automatic (perplexity, MAUVE, diversity); human assessment would strengthen claims about perceived generation quality improvements

Incomplete analysis of error predictor: No false negative analysis showing which errors are missed, limited exploration of failure modes under severe distribution shift, and sensitivity to predictor capacity thresholds unclear

ReMDM comparison complexity: While criticizing ReMDM's hyperparameter sensitivity, G-Star also requires tuning (τremask, ton); the comparison could be more balanced in highlighting inherent difficulty of both approaches

Design choices not fully justified: Error predictor trained on different datasets for different tasks (OWT, Tulu 3); impact of this inconsistency unexplored, generalization to universal error predictor unclear
